intro: AI UGC is a creator-style ad made without booking a crew. An avatar delivers a short review, a demo, or a first look at the package, in the frame that app already uses. You still supply the product photo and the claim you can stand behind.

faq.q: Why do shoppers buy from creator-style AI ads?
faq.a: A shopper pauses when the clip sounds like someone talking about a product they use, and the item is visible in the first second. For a lip oil, show the wand before any slogan. A tall frame helps on a full-screen app, but the pause comes from the product being obvious.
An AI UGC ad is a short clip where an AI actor talks about your item in a casual way. You still supply the product photo and the claim. Nobody has to come to your storeroom with a camera.

faq.q: Can I try a clip before I pick a larger plan?
faq.a: You start on a paid plan. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, which covers stills at 24 credits and short videos from 24 credits. Nothing has to be filmed first.

faq.q: How long should I plan for one AI UGC ad?
faq.a: There is no shoot date to book. Paste the listing or a photo of the item and pick an AI actor. Read the finished file on a phone before you put spend behind it.

faq.q: How do I make a UGC ad with an AI avatar?
faq.a: Start from the product you can photograph today, then choose an adult face from the actor library. Read the draft out loud. If the claim is one you can support, export the frame the app expects.

faq.q: Where do the presenters for these ads come from?
faq.a: They come from the actor library. You pick a face, and that person holds your item and says the line. You do not book a studio.

faq.q: Can a product page become the UGC ad?
faq.a: Yes. A public page for the tote is enough to start. You still read the line before you post it, and you add the price yourself if the page price is wrong.

faq.q: Are commercial rights included when the ad is AI-made?
faq.a: Yes. A file you make on a paid plan can run as an ad, and the download has no watermark. Use your own logo file only if you have the right to put it on the clip.

faq.q: After a video is generated, can I still change it?
faq.a: Yes. If the avatar calls your mug leakproof and you have not tested that, change the line before you post. You can also pick a different face for a second file.

faq.q: How is filmed UGC unlike the AI version?
faq.a: Filmed UGC needs a person, a time, and a place. The AI version uses an actor from the library and your product photo, so a second hook is another job rather than another afternoon. Use the filmed piece when you want a specific person your buyers already know.

faq.q: Can AI UGC replace a human creator?
faq.a: Use it when you need several openings for the same blender. If the ad only works because a founder your buyers already follow is on camera, film that person and keep the AI clips for the other products.

faq.q: How many languages can these channel ads use?
faq.a: As many as the countries you ship to. You can record a version for the next country and keep the same product shots. If you want the voice to match a person on your team, supply a short sample of that person.
English, Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, and Hindi are among the choices, and you can ask if a market you sell in is missing.

faq.q: What if the ad has to be ready before a launch date?
faq.a: Start from the product page or a photo you already have, and skip booking a crew. Mute the file and fix any caption that names the wrong shade.

faq.q: Can I clone a voice for these channel ads?
faq.a: Yes. Record a few sentences in a quiet room and use that voice on the avatar. A later ad for the same shop can keep it, so two clips from that shop can sound like one person.

faq.q: Can the ads go out with no creator on payroll?
faq.a: Yes. The test can go out with an AI actor from the library and a photo of the item. You pay the plan, not a creator day rate.

faq.q: How does an AI UGC ad get made?
faq.a: You bring the product photo. The tool writes a line from what you say is true, an AI actor delivers it, and you fix any word that overclaims before you download.

faq.q: Can I get a testimonial, a demo, and a TikTok-style clip from this?
faq.a: Yes. A testimonial can be one sentence about who the item is for. A demo can be the lid coming off. An unboxing can stop when the item is fully visible. Pick one of those for the file, and start from a photo if you do not want to paste a page.

faq.q: What should I look for in an AI UGC tool?
faq.a: Look for a tool that starts from the product you already sell and hands you a file you can post. On AIVideosUGC a failed job returns the credits.

m2.h2: How to Make a File for One App in 3 Steps

m3.h2: Ads for Each App You Sell On
m3.lead: Open the app you post on. TikTok, Instagram Reels, Facebook, YouTube Shorts, Amazon, and Shopify each show the shape they expect.

benefits_h2: What You Can Make for a Channel

benefits.d: A ceramic mug photo on your phone is enough. Ask for a square catalog still and a short clip of the mug on a breakfast table. Both come back in this project.
You get a clip you can play from a short brief. Say you sell a linen apron to home cooks and you want a calm kitchen, and you can change one word before you export.
You can reuse an opening you already like, with your own product in the frame. A reel that starts on a hand turning a jar can do that with your hot sauce, and the line can name the heat.
You can start the ad from the store page you already have. The tote shows in three colors there, and the line can name the strap length.
You can stay off camera and still have someone holding the product and reading the line.
Next week's launch can use your face while you pack orders. Film one clear clip of yourself holding the headphones, and save that face.

steps_h2: How to Make a File for One App in 3 Steps
steps_lead: You leave with a file the ad account can take.

steps.d: Open a project and say who the bottle is for, like a buyer who hates sticky sunscreen. One bottle photo is all you need.
It may ask whether the moisturizer is mineral or chemical. Answer that, and keep the line on a white cast if your formula has one.
Download the moisturizer clip and drop it into the ad account you already use. You can also send it from the project.

directory_specs.title: Frames You Can Export for Each App
directory_specs.lead: You export the frame that app already expects. A square still is the default photo. Video can be 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4, and you can add a voice, on-screen text, and music.

The Shorts shelf
Choose a 6, 10, 15, or 30-second tall clip. Add a voice and captions when the action needs them, then upload the download to Shorts.
Amazon
Listing photos, or a video ad

Square stills, and video in 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4. You attach the files on the listing.
Shopify
The product gallery
Square photos
Square stills, plus a clip at 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds in 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4. Drop them into the product in your store admin.

reasons.h2: Why Sellers Make AI Ads by Platform
reasons.lead: The product stays yours. The frame, the language, and the finish change with the app.

items.d: The face can match the shopper you are talking to, and that same face can front the ad on every channel. The library covers different ages and looks.
The next market hears the ad in their own language, with the same product shots. An avatar can use a voice you supply.
You can ask for help while a launch is in motion, so a stuck export does not eat the afternoon.
One project covers the next app. A square cut of the same candle unboxing fits a Facebook feed once the tall file is done, and the spoken line stays.
Rendering finishes fast enough to catch a launch window. You can post while the offer is still the one on the site.
Your label color and corner mark land on both the tall clip and the square still. Set them once, and a serum bottle keeps that label color.

trust.h2: Who Uses AI Ads for Each Platform
trust.lead: Different shops, the same job: a finished ad for the channel that takes the order.

items.d: A home-goods shop can put the vase on a side table in a clip, then try a second opening line on the next file. Orders on the site do not wait for that test.
Spin a new listing into a native-style clip before you decide the product is worth more ad spend.
The person who runs a two-person soap shop can have an avatar hold the bar and name the scent. That keeps a post going out on the week the owner is at a market.
Produce a fresh cut for each client channel, keep the brand rules, and spend your time on the offer.
Use an AI twin so the posting schedule does not depend on another afternoon in front of the phone.
A feature can be explained from a screen recording you already have. An avatar can say what the file is for, and the last frame can point at your install page.

more_sections.lead: Shoppers already pause for these shapes, and the product stays easy to recognize.

items.d: One reason to buy, said the way a cook would post it. The avatar can say why this maple syrup stays next to the stove, such as it stays thick on pancakes.
The annoyance comes first, then the product clears it. Start with a sweater that pills after one wash, show the comb lifting the pills, and end on the clean knit.
A travel mug clip can show the lid twist and the sip. The line can name those two moves, which a buyer can see.

items.t: A First Look at the Box
items.d: The open can match the mailer you actually send. Show that mailer, then the tissue, then the candle.

more_sections.h2: Edit Your Platform Ad in One Place
more_sections.lead: Adjust the picture, the words, and the next cut in the same place you made the ad.

items.d: You can change one word and export again, without a second editor. The apron clip can say one pocket when that is what you sell.
You can update the on-screen date when the sale moves, and match the letters to the product. A denim jacket clip can use the same indigo as the patch.
The same face can whisper on one cut and sound surprised on the next. A quiet line fits a jewelry story, and a brighter line can land on the clasp.
A second hook or a second ratio comes from the same product when the first file is tired.

reviews.h2: How a Shop Uses Each Channel
reviews.lead: Examples of how a shop would use it, not quotes from named customers.

items.d: A TikTok seller makes a tall 9:16 video with a spoken line and captions, then sends it to TikTok or downloads it.
A shop that posts Reels uses a tall 9:16 file. If the post list wants 4:5, they crop the square photo in the editor.
A Facebook shop makes a square photo for the post list and a separate tall 9:16 video for the full-screen spot.
A Shorts seller picks tall 9:16 and 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds, with captions for the one action.
A marketplace seller starts with a square photo, then adds a video beside the photo gallery.
A store owner keeps gallery photos square and adds a short video when motion explains the product.

closing.h2: Know the Cost Before You Render
paras: Play the cut with the sound off and read the captions before you put money behind it. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. The balances are on the [pricing page](page:pricing).
A still is 24 credits. A video is 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. The cost is on screen before the job starts. A failed job returns the credits.

definition.title: What Is AI UGC
paras: AI UGC is a creator-style ad made from your product photo. An AI avatar says a line you approve, with captions and a voice, and you did not book a crew.
You can start from a listing link or from one still. The file can be a review, a short demo, or a first look at the package, in the frame the app already uses.
